Q1.answer: When several LLM agents share a memory, each query must be routed to some agent's memory; searching every agent (global search) costs tokens on every query. The paper measures whether routing each query to an agent that has learned 'ownership' of the query's topic can cut that per-query token cost, what it does to answer quality, and how it copes when a new topic appears.

Q2.answer: Global search pays the token cost of consulting every candidate on every query, so cost grows with the size of the shared memory; a cheaper routing scheme matters if it does not lose answer quality. The paper asserts the cost framing but gives little argument for why the absolute saving matters in practice (the tested budgets are about 180 tokens per query), and it mentions but does not state the authors' reason for prioritising cost and answerability over accuracy.
Q2.missing: The authors' stated reason for foregrounding cost is referenced but not given; no practical-scale argument for why about 40 tokens per query matters.

Q3.answer: The paper frames the gap as one of measurement: what learned ownership saves compared with global search, what it costs in answer quality, and how it behaves under topic change. It explicitly cannot say what existing published methods lack, because no literature search was run. It only notes that supervised classifier routers regain a new topic only after a retrain.
Q3.missing: No comparison with published routing, memory, expert-finding or reputation methods, so what is missing from existing approaches cannot be determined from the paper.

Q4.answer: They ran ASMOS, a shared-memory layer whose routing score is query-to-agent similarity multiplied by the agent's learned ownership of the topic, with a fallback to global search below a threshold. They compared four arms (A0 global search, A1 ownership learned from verified outcomes, A2 ownership frozen at its prior, A3 similarity only) on a constructed 50-query, two-agent corpus with gpt-4o-mini and 10 seeds. They also ran a new-topic adaptation experiment against frozen and periodically retrained classifier routers with two embedders, and a single-run static QA comparison (No-Memory, RAG, ASMOS-memory, ASMOS+RAG) on 24 RULER items.

Q5.answer: For the system itself the paper gives no design rationale. For the analysis it does: bootstrap CI over queries because query heterogeneity dominates; one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank with zero differences dropped to keep a pre-registered p-value; rank-biserial effect size as the signed-rank test's companion with a single definition; n_eff reported to prevent misreading r = 1.0; A2 as a single-variable ablation; classifier baselines as the supervised alternative for new topics.
Q5.missing: Why ownership times similarity, why verification-gated reputation, and why these particular baselines (for example no online-updated classifier) are not justified.

Q6.answer: (1) Cost experiment: 4 routing arms, 50 queries in five classes, two agents, gpt-4o-mini at temperature 0, 10 seeds, measuring LLM tokens per query, context tokens, candidate-set size, accuracy, answerability and route@1 (per-seed secondary measures only for seeds 66 to 110). (2) New-topic adaptation: 10 steps, 5 evaluation queries per step, 5 seeds, two embedders (all-mpnet-base-v2, bge-m3), ASMOS against frozen, every-5 and every-10 retrained classifiers, measured by cumulative regret in route@1. (3) A single stationary run comparing MiniLM and a lexical-hash embedder against a classifier. (4) Static QA: 4 systems, 24 RULER items, one run, exact match, token-F1 and tokens.

Q7.answer: A1 used 22.1% fewer LLM total tokens per query than global search (180.2 to 140.4), with a bootstrap 95% CI of 17.9% to 26.3%, per-seed reductions of 21.9% to 22.2%, Wilcoxon W = 1141.5, p = 6.8e-9, r = 0.941 over 48 non-zero pairs. Answerability was equal at 0.98. In the new-topic regime ASMOS had regret 3.24 (mpnet) and 0.92 (bge-m3) with no retrains, against 4.8, 9.0 and 10.0 for classifiers.

Q8.answer: On this constructed two-agent corpus with gpt-4o-mini, routing to a learned owner reliably reduced per-query token use by roughly a fifth, with query-level uncertainty of about plus or minus 4 points, without lowering answerability but with slightly lower accuracy (1 to 2 of 50 questions) in the recorded seeds. Freezing ownership at its prior removes the saving, which is consistent with, not proof of, ownership updates producing it. In one small new-topic setup, ASMOS reached the new owner without retraining and had lower mean regret than the scheduled classifiers tested.

Q9.answer: Not established: a saving rate for organic workloads or other answering models; the size (or even reliability) of the accuracy cost, since there is no paired test and grading is undocumented; that ownership evolution specifically causes the saving (A2 simply falls back to global search, and there is no test for A1 against A2); statistically supported regret superiority or budget parity with the classifiers; any QA-accuracy benefit of ASMOS (it scored below no-memory and RAG); faster or more sample-efficient ownership learning; anything about labelling cost; results at team sizes beyond two agents.

Q10.answer: A carefully bounded measurement of the token saving from ownership-based routing in shared LLM-agent memory (22.1%, CI 17.9% to 26.3%), reported together with its accuracy cost, an ablation, and new-topic adaptation behaviour, rather than a new method positioned against prior work.

Q11.answer: Deliberately constructed corpus with built-in ownership asymmetry and only two agents; one answering model; half of the seeds come from a missing result file; the earliest run's embedder is unconfirmed; the routing threshold was tuned on the same corpus; accuracy grading is undocumented and untested; the ablation has no test; classifier tuning is undocumented; small new-topic runs (5 seeds, 5 queries per step) with strong embedder dependence; static QA is a single run of 24 items; corpus, queries and code are unavailable; no literature positioning.

Q12.answer: Routing queries to an agent that has learned topic ownership saved about 22% of LLM tokens against asking every agent, on a constructed benchmark, with slightly lower accuracy; it is a cost and routing tool, not a way to answer questions better.
